tier_reason: README 'Benchmark results' table gives bin-mean speedups vs std::sort, pdqsort, ska_sort, IPS4o and vqsort produced by the public driver benchmark/main_bigdata.cpp (with competitors.hpp, datagen.hpp, bench_engine.hpp and benchmark/CMakeLists.txt), and states g++ 13.2, -O3 -mavx2 -mbmi -DNDEBUG and Intel Core i5-12400F. The driver checks every run's output against a std::sort reference and logs an ok/FAIL column, so the timings are of real sorts.

corrections.caveats: Very new single-author repo (7 commits, 2026-05-09 to 2026-08-07, 32 stars); all numbers from one Windows 11 desktop (i5-12400F, AVX2 path only, no AVX-512 run of vqsort). std::sort is libstdc++ (inferred from the g++ 13.2 toolchain; the README does not name the library). Timings are best of 2 runs per (N, K) point with high_resolution_clock, on uint64 keys drawn from a K-value palette spread over the 64-bit range; only the u64 path is benchmarked although int32/int64 specializations exist. The raw CSV is not in the repo (README says it ships with the preprint artifact); arXiv 2605.25040 exists (seen via a search snippet only, arXiv blocked) and is not peer reviewed. The README is internally inconsistent about std::sort: its crossover line says std::sort reaches parity at K = 1.7e7, while the table shows 3.47x for that bin and the operational table says CAFS still wins at K = N. CAFS loses to vqsort (0.60x) and ska_sort (0.66x) near K = N, and the dispatcher's worst case is about 5x pdqsort time. A 'signed-radix fix' landed on 2026-05-09 but does not touch the u64 path measured. This is a sorting library; it fits the existing 'sorting' category better than simd-intrinsics-libraries.

notes: Numbers match the README table exactly; benchmark code is public, verifies correctness and uses fair std::function wrappers for every algorithm. Shortcomings: one desktop CPU, best of 2 runs, raw CSV not published, README contradicts itself on the std::sort crossover, slower than vqsort and ska_sort when K approaches N. Suggest a category override to 'sorting'.

tier_reason: README tables time qReverse against std::reverse with the public harness tests/benchmark.cpp (CMakeLists.txt builds it with -march=native -Ofast for GCC), on an Intel Core i3-6100 compiled with g++ -m64 -Ofast -march=native. The g++ version is not stated, which weakens but does not remove reproducibility.

corrections.claimed_speedup: i3-6100, g++ -m64 -Ofast -march=native, 1-byte elements, bswap variant vs std::reverse: 1000 elements 290 ns vs 36 ns (8.056x); 10000: 2740 vs 191 ns (14.346x); 100000: 27511 vs 1739 ns (15.820x); 1,000,000: 279525 vs 24710 ns (11.312x); 8 elements 19 vs 19 ns (1.000x). SSSE3 variant peaks at 10.510x (10000 elements) and the AVX2 variant at 16.053x (100000 elements: 27515 vs 1714 ns). AVX512 on i9-7900x, built with Visual Studio 2017 x64-Release: peak 22.357x at 10000 elements (2504 vs 112 ns), 11.153x at 1,000,000. The top-of-README speedup table (AVX2 x22.032 and AVX512 x22.357 on i9-7900x, AVX2 x16.053 on i3-6100) lists peak speedups over std::reverse (the 'Serial' x1 column); the i3-6100 and i9-7900x AVX512 values equal the peaks of the std::reverse tables (derived from page data), while the i5-8600K, E5-2697 v4 and BCM2837 rows have no table or flags behind them.
corrections.workload: Reversing arrays of 1-byte elements (ELEMENTSIZE=1 struct of one uint8_t) of 8 to 1,000,000 elements; each size gets 10,000 back-to-back reversals of the same in-cache array, each call timed individually with high_resolution_clock and averaged, std::reverse vs qReverse<1>.
corrections.caveats: Numbers are from 2017-2018 (last README benchmark update 2018-10-30) with an unstated g++ version; newer GCC/Clang may vectorize std::reverse better. Per-call timing with high_resolution_clock means rows under about 30 ns are dominated by clock overhead (8 elements: 19 ns vs 19 ns). The benchmark does not check the reversed output (correctness is covered by the separate tests/verify.cpp). The AVX512 table on i9-7900x was built with Visual Studio 2017 x64-Release (MSVC STL baseline, exact flags not given); the i5-8600K, E5-2697 v4 and Raspberry Pi BCM2837 speedups are listed without tables or flags. Only 1-byte elements are tabulated, although the harness supports 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16-byte elements. Abandoned since 2018-12-19.

notes: All claimed numbers are on the README; there are three i3-6100 std::reverse tables (bswap, SSSE3, AVX2) plus an MSVC i9-7900x AVX512 table, not only the bswap one. Shortcomings: unstated g++ version, 2018-era numbers, per-call timing noise at small sizes, other CPUs' speedups have no backing table, abandoned.

tier_reason: For the SSE4 rows: the public harness main.c times naive, lookup (Hoehrmann DFA), Lemire SSE and range/range2 over 1 GB per case, the Makefile sets -O3 -march=native, the README says built and tested with gcc-7.3, and the table names the Intel Xeon E5-2650. The NEON table names no CPU model (only armv8a), so it would be C on its own.

corrections.caveats: Same algorithm and same README tables as the wave 3 entry https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf ('utf8_range (SIMD Range-based UTF-8 validator)'); protobuf's third_party/utf8_range/README.md is a copy of this README. This repo is the original research code. The benchmark tables date from November 2018 and predate the September 2020 optimizations of both the range code (x86 port of NEON optimizations) and the lookup baseline ('lookup: use a more optimized variant'), so the lookup column is stale. A 2020 fix (commit 31cf77b) corrected main.c so lemire_avx2 no longer ran range_avx2; no AVX2 table is published, so the tables are unaffected. E5-2650 generation (v1-v4) is not stated. On SSE4 the range algorithm only ties Lemire's 2018 prototype and loses at 32-byte buffers (2173.02 or 2351.81 vs 2890.52 MB/s); the real wins are over the naive loop (3.1x at 1 MB) and the lookup DFA (12.8x), and on NEON over Lemire's port (1.32x). simdutf, already catalogued, is the newer and broader implementation. Last code commit 2020-10-27; last commit 2025-09-07 (README usage note).

notes: Duplicate of the already-verified wave 3 record https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf (utf8_range), which reproduces this README's tables verbatim; record decision 'duplicate'. Consider re-pointing that wave 3 record's repo_url and benchmark_url to https://github.com/cyb70289/utf8 (the original repo, with main.c and Makefile) and retiering it from C to A for the x86 SSE4 rows, since this repo states gcc-7.3, -O3 -march=native and the E5-2650 (the wave 3 caveat 'no optimization flags' is answered by the Makefile).
